Not mentioned anywhere in this story or the article: ANY ANALYSIS AT ALL of the relative cost in dollars per watt of these panels versus just building solar farms on empty land.

These sorts of projects have some value if your primary goal is reducing evaporation (or reducing urban heat island effects by covering parking lots, or whatever). But if your goal is reducing climate change and/or reducing dependency on fossil fuels, they are honestly kind of terrible. 

For the same cost you can build, VERY conservatively, four times as much capacity in the Mojave desert. Those numbers actually come from parking lot structures - building over water is surely more expensive. (How much more expensive? I don't know, because this story doesn't address economics AT ALL.)

It's a dramatic enough difference that, even if shading the canals is an important priority, it might be better economics to build lightweight shading that goes over the canals *AND* build more solar farms in the Mojave desert, rather than building these panels.

But these sorts of questions aren't even being addressed here. Without that sort of breakdown, this is more of a "feels good" story than a real analysis of what should/will happen and why.

(Eventually as we get better at building lightweight thin-film solar panels, the cost for these sorts of power-generating shade structures will come down and then they will start to become much more prevalent. But right now, these structures are in the same place that solar generation was 25 years ago - a technology that technically works but isn't economically competitive.)

This story isn't about *all* the locations where solar can be installed - they're already rolling it out in agricultural fields where I live. The story is about a specific situation - using space that is otherwise unused to solve at least two problems (generating power + preventing water loss), while assessing any new problems (maintenance and cost, etc) that may emerge with the solution. 

To me, those structures look a little over-engineered - yes, panels have weight and need to be properly secured - but perhaps they're looking at the kind of inputs that will inform the structure design in specific situations/locations. 

The concerns some people had re narrower canals didn't make sense to me either - build narrower structures. Solar panels are modular units, after all, and can be assembled in all kinds of shapes. If access is too difficult, fine, don't build there. There will also be a formula needed to calculate if too many "gaps" in your deployment make it too inefficient, but for a long array, I doubt there will be a single exit point for exporting the electricity. Probably needs a formula to figure out if a section is "long enough" for the conditions and can be readily connected for export.

You need to block the wind coming in low from the sides as well if you want to stop evaporation. Shade is nice, but the real killer isn't the direct sunlight, it's dry air blowing in and replacing the saturated air sitting over the water. You need to stop that dry air from blowing in. Either block it with a solid wall from ground level up to the roof so the canal is flowing inside a fully enclosed shed, or else look into a perforated wall or a hedge to slow the air movement without creating turbulence over the water.
Your other option is a big pipe. Pipes are pretty good at not losing water to evaporation, but then there won't be any evaporation at all to cool your solar panels.

It is not entirely that simple: The water evaporating from the canals goes somewhere. Where does it go? Into the surrounding air. Why does it go there? Because the surrounding hot air is dry, "sucking in" any water it can find. Keeping the canal water cooler makes it harder for the water to evaporate, so the surrounding air stays dryer which increases the power it wants to suck in water with. Where else is water? In the plants on the fields. If the air is dryer, the plants evaporate more water to the air. So for the same result in health and growth, they need more irrigation and hence - surprise! - water.

That big about 'cheating' emissions tests is more of an aside, but I kind of wonder how many cash for clunkers vehicles would've passed SMOG tests if fueled up with E30 or E35 ... except a lot of those also included early 80s era V8s with the dreaded electronic control carburetors, and if the metering rods go bad in those, you really need a carb rebuild to get that working. (unless they're stuck in rich, in which case the alcohol blend MIGHT be enough to fix things by shifting that into the near-perfect lambda 1.0 stiochiometric point when in cruise: the carb's accelerator pump squirts extra fuel to enrich the mixture when you initially press down on the throttle pedal, but having stoich AFR in steady-state throttle position would get you to low emissions if the catalytic converter is working even if EGR and air injection is messed up). To be fair, it's not really cheating if you run that ethanol blend all the time, which one could usually get away with if you have E85 stations locally.  (running normal pump gas, especially 87 ocane, at that same lamda of 1.0 might cause knock in those same engines at full throttle, which is why EGR dilution and/or rich mixture is used and with rich mixture you need air injection for the cat to work right, but with around E30 to E35, even 87 octane pump gas becomes closer to 93 or 94 octane AKI or likely around 100~101 RON 87~88 MON ... it's not a simple rule of mixtures as ethanol's blending ON is higher than its neat ON, and the lower octane the base stock is, the more impact the alcohol has, and the higher ON the base stock then the less dramatic the blending ON is with ethanol, and methanol is also like this; that also makes such blends unsuitable for the European RON pump rating as they mandate that the MON must be no more than 10 points lower than RON, albeit you could legally rate 100/88 RON/MON as 98 octane fuel in the UK and Europe for that reason)  


Also both methanol and butanol are efficient to produce from syngas (the latter has lower yields, but higher value for gasoline blending due to energy density and low hygroscopicity, so it can be pipelined and now attract too much moisture where methanol and ethanol need to be trucked in and blended straight at the fuel station). Butanol can also be made through fermentation of carbohydrates and some other biomass (both the 120 year old Weisman process using ABE fermentation, plus more modern derivatives and engineered strains of e. coli that can broduce the more desireable isobutanol, the same isomer that syngas based mixed alcohol synthesis produces). Butanol or mixed higher alcohols can also be made from the light to medium olefin fractions of crude oil or from crude oil cracking processes, and would be lower carbon footprint and cheaper (and higher yield) to produce than using those same fractions to produce alkylate (a high octane branched hydrocarbon fuel). Low grade oil byproducts and flare gas could be used as cheap syngas sources as well. (though natural gas is the cheapest and lowest carbon source for syngas from fossil fuel sources, albeit you can use waste CO2 from oilrefining and natural gas to dry-reform CO2 into syngas rather than using steam reforming, and thus reduce the carbon footprint compared to steam reforming; albeit you need surplus waste heat to drive the endothermic dry reforming process vs the exothermic steam reforming, but plenty of synthetic fuel processes are highly exothermic, including methanol synthesis, mixed alcohol synthesis and fischer-tropsch synthesis ... and hydration of olefins is also exothermic, but not dramatically so)


Olefins are the same as alkenes, the latter is the formal scientific term used in organic chemistry, the former is an antiquated term still used in petrochemical industrial contexts, plus organic chemistry texts from around 100 years ago.

Ground mounted solar PV arrays has been criticized for clearing and stealing arable land that could be used for agriculture.  This criticism is astounding considering that forest are mainly burned and cleared for cattle ranching; which is the leading cause of deforestation.  
However, ground mounted solar PV arrays can coexist along with agriculture and livestock.  This dual purpose use of land provides a symbiotic relationship for energy production and agriculture; giving family owned and cooperative farmers another sustainable revenue stream.   
Through transpiration, the plants below keep the array cool boosting power production.  Already on agrivoltaic farms livestock are grazing on pasture growing under elevated ground mounted solar arrays.  Plants benefit from the shade of the array and are shielded from heavy rains, hail and sun stress.  
Plants do have a limit on the amount of sunshine they can metabolize known as light saturation point.  Once a plant reaches this maximum rate of photosynthesis the plant starts evaporating water to cool itself.  Agrivoltaics reduce the amount of water evaporation from plants reducing water loss and agricultural water usage.
